# Computing Correlation Functions at Finite Momenta in the Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group

The calculation of n-point correlation functions at finite momenta represents a central challenge in the application of Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) methods. The conventional strategy for addressing this problem relies on truncating the infinite hierarchy of flow equations by including only a finite number of vertices. In practice, this means that one restricts attention to a limited set of correlation functions, closing the system of equations at some chosen order and thereby rendering the problem tractable. While this approach has proven useful in many contexts, its reliability depends sensitively on the order at which the truncation is performed.

In the present work, we adopt a recently introduced general method that departs from this traditional scheme. Rather than retaining only a finite number of vertices, this approach incorporates all vertices simultaneously, at the cost of introducing an approximation for their momentum dependence. This reorganization of the computation allows one to capture contributions that would otherwise be discarded in a standard finite-order truncation, offering a potentially more faithful description of the full momentum structure of the correlation functions.

To assess the performance of this method, we focus our analysis on the self-energy of the three-dimensional scalar model at criticality. This system provides an ideal testing ground, as it is both physically relevant and sufficiently well understood that the accuracy of any approximation scheme can be reliably benchmarked against known results.

Our findings reveal that the order of truncation plays a decisive role in the quality of the results. Low-order truncations can lead to substantial errors in the determination of physical quantities. In particular, the critical exponent η is found to be significantly misestimated at low orders, with deviations reaching as much as 60%. Such large discrepancies underscore the inadequacy of low-order approximations for obtaining quantitatively accurate predictions in this context.

By contrast, extending the calculation to higher-order truncations dramatically improves the situation. As the order of truncation is increased, the procedure exhibits rapid convergence, with successive approximations quickly approaching a stable result. This behavior demonstrates that the method is well controlled and capable of delivering reliable, high-precision results when carried to sufficiently high order, thereby validating its use for the computation of correlation functions at finite momenta.

# Truncation Schemes in Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group Calculations of Correlation Functions

## Introduction

The Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) provides a powerful framework for studying strongly correlated systems and critical phenomena beyond the reach of perturbative methods. At its core, the NPRG formalism generates an infinite hierarchy of coupled flow equations for the vertex functions of a theory. Computing n-point correlation functions at finite external momenta—rather than merely in the zero-momentum limit—represents one of the most demanding applications of this approach, as it requires careful treatment of the full momentum dependence of the vertices.

The conventional strategy for making these calculations tractable is truncation: the infinite hierarchy of flow equations is closed by retaining only a finite number of vertices, discarding higher-order vertex functions. While this approach has yielded valuable results, an important question remains regarding its systematic reliability. In particular, it is essential to understand how the accuracy of physical predictions depends on the order at which the truncation is performed.

## Method

To address this question, we employ a recently developed method that takes a complementary approach to the standard truncation. Rather than discarding higher vertices, this method retains all vertices in the hierarchy while introducing a controlled approximation for their momentum dependence. This strategy allows us to construct an effectively "complete" reference calculation against which finite-vertex truncations can be systematically benchmarked.

We apply this framework to a concrete and physically significant example: the self-energy of the three-dimensional critical scalar field model. This system belongs to the Ising universality class in three dimensions and serves as a canonical testing ground for renormalization group techniques, owing to its well-characterized critical behavior and the availability of high-precision results from other methods for comparison.

## Results

Our analysis yields two central findings that together clarify the trustworthiness of the truncation procedure.

First, we find that **low-order truncations can be substantially unreliable**. When the flow equations are closed by retaining only a small number of vertices, physical observables can deviate dramatically from their correct values. In particular, the anomalous dimension—encoded in the critical exponent η—can be misestimated by as much as 60%. This is a striking discrepancy that underscores the danger of drawing quantitative conclusions from truncations carried out at insufficient order.

Second, and more encouragingly, we observe **rapid convergence at high orders of truncation**. As additional vertices are included, the computed quantities converge quickly toward stable values. This fast convergence demonstrates that the truncation scheme, while unreliable at low orders, becomes robust and accurate once carried to sufficiently high order.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these results establish both the limitations and the reliability of the standard truncation approach within the NPRG framework. The large errors seen at low order caution against the naive use of minimal truncations for quantitative predictions of momentum-dependent correlation functions. At the same time, the rapid convergence at higher orders confirms that the truncation procedure is fundamentally sound and can deliver accurate results when applied systematically. By using a method that incorporates all vertices as a benchmark, we provide clear evidence that carrying the truncation to sufficient order restores the predictive power of the approach, thereby validating its continued use in the study of critical phenomena and other non-perturbative problems.

# The Non-Perturbative Realm of Physics

## Introduction

In theoretical physics, the term **non-perturbative** describes phenomena and mathematical techniques that cannot be captured by perturbation theory—the standard approach of expanding solutions as a power series in a small parameter. While perturbative methods have driven enormous success in fields like quantum electrodynamics, they fundamentally fail to describe certain crucial aspects of nature.

## Understanding the Distinction

Perturbation theory works by treating a complex problem as a small deviation from a simpler, solvable one. Physicists expand quantities in powers of a coupling constant, keeping terms up to a desired order. This works beautifully when interactions are weak.

However, many important effects **vanish to all orders** in perturbation theory. These non-perturbative contributions typically involve factors like:

$$e^{-1/g^2}$$

where *g* is the coupling constant. Such expressions are smooth but have a mathematical "essential singularity" that no Taylor expansion can reproduce.

## Where Non-Perturbative Effects Matter

Several fundamental phenomena are inherently non-perturbative:

- **Quark confinement** — The reason quarks are never observed in isolation cannot be explained by perturbative Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD).
- **Instantons** — Localized solutions to field equations that contribute to tunneling between vacuum states.
- **Solitons and monopoles** — Stable, particle-like field configurations.
- **Spontaneous symmetry breaking** — Certain aspects of vacuum structure.

## Methods and Approaches

Physicists have developed powerful tools to probe the non-perturbative domain:

1. **Lattice field theory** — Discretizing spacetime to enable numerical computation.
2. **Supersymmetric field theories** — Exploiting symmetries to obtain exact results.
3. **Holographic dualities** — The AdS/CFT correspondence relates strongly coupled theories to gravitational systems.
4. **Semiclassical expansions** — Building approximations around non-trivial classical solutions.

## Conclusion

The non-perturbative frontier remains one of the most challenging and rewarding areas of modern physics. It holds the keys to understanding phenomena that shape our universe at the deepest levels—from the confinement of quarks inside protons to the very structure of the quantum vacuum. As computational and mathematical techniques advance, this once-inaccessible realm continues to reveal its profound secrets.

# Abstract

We present a systematic analysis of vertex truncation schemes employed in the Non-Perturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) framework for the computation of higher-order n-point correlation functions. The exact flow equations of the effective average action generate an infinite hierarchy of coupled equations for the one-particle-irreducible vertices, necessitating truncations that inevitably introduce systematic errors. In this work, we investigate the convergence properties and reliability of successive vertex expansion orders by comparing truncations that retain vertices up to the four-, six-, and eight-point functions. Focusing on scalar field theories in the symmetric and broken phases, we quantify the impact of neglecting higher vertices on the momentum dependence of the two- and four-point functions, with particular attention to the infrared regime where non-perturbative effects dominate. Our results demonstrate that the accuracy of computed correlation functions depends sensitively on the interplay between the truncation order and the choice of regulator, and we identify regimes in which apparent convergence may mask residual truncation artifacts. We further assess the role of field-dependent versus field-independent vertex approximations and their consequences for critical exponents and anomalous dimensions. These findings provide practical guidelines for controlling systematic uncertainties in NPRG calculations and establish benchmarks for the extraction of reliable n-point functions in strongly correlated systems.

# NPRG Truncation Schemes for the 3D Scalar Model Self-Energy

## Context and Motivation

The Nonperturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) provides a powerful framework for studying critical phenomena in scalar field theories. A key challenge is accurately computing the **anomalous dimension η**, which characterizes the momentum dependence of the two-point function (self-energy) at criticality and is one of the more difficult critical exponents to determine precisely.

## Key Aspects of the Research

### Truncation Schemes

Research in this area typically compares several approximation strategies:

- **Derivative Expansion (DE):** Expands the effective action in powers of momentum/derivatives. While reliable for exponents like ν, it captures η only through the field renormalization factor Zₖ, limiting access to full momentum dependence.

- **BMW (Blaizot–Méndez-Galain–Wschebor) scheme:** Retains the full momentum dependence of correlation functions, making it particularly suited for computing the self-energy across all scales rather than just its low-momentum behavior.

- **Vertex expansions:** Truncate the hierarchy of flow equations at a given order in the fields, with varying treatments of momentum structure.

### Convergence Behavior

The main findings generally emphasize:

- **Systematic improvement** with successive orders of the derivative expansion, showing apparent convergence of η toward accepted values, though often more slowly than for other exponents.

- **Momentum-dependent schemes** (like BMW) provide better control over the self-energy's structure, especially in the crossover between infrared and ultraviolet regimes.

- The choice of **regulator function** significantly affects intermediate results, with optimization principles (e.g., the principle of minimal sensitivity) used to identify optimal values.

### Critical Exponent η

For the 3D Ising universality class (N=1 scalar model):
- Reference values place **η ≈ 0.036**
- Higher-order truncations and full momentum schemes converge toward these values
- η is especially sensitive to how faithfully the momentum dependence of the self-energy is preserved, making it a stringent test of any truncation scheme

---

**Note:** I've provided a general summary based on established knowledge of NPRG methodology. If you have a **specific paper** in mind, please share the title, authors, or key details, and I can tailor this summary to that particular work—including its precise numerical results, novel truncation proposals, and specific conclusions.

counterfactuals.prompt: I'm studying functional renormalization group methods. Can you explain how truncating the number of vertices affects the accuracy of critical exponents like eta, using the tridimensional scalar model as an example?
counterfactuals.output:
# Truncations in the FRG and Critical Exponents

The functional renormalization group (FRG), typically formulated via the Wetterich equation for the effective average action Γ_k, is exact in principle but requires truncation for practical calculations. Understanding how truncation affects η is a great way to see the method's structure.

## The Wetterich Equation and the Need for Truncation

The flow equation reads:

$$\partial_t \Gamma_k = \frac{1}{2}\text{Tr}\left[\left(\Gamma_k^{(2)} + R_k\right)^{-1} \partial_t R_k\right]$$

where $t = \ln(k/\Lambda)$. This generates an infinite hierarchy: the flow of the n-point vertex $\Gamma^{(n)}$ depends on $\Gamma^{(n+1)}$ and $\Gamma^{(n+2)}$. You must truncate somewhere.

## Two Main Truncation Schemes

**1. Derivative Expansion**
Organizes Γ_k by powers of momentum/derivatives:

$$\Gamma_k = \int d^dx\left[U_k(\phi) + \frac{1}{2}Z_k(\phi)(\partial\phi)^2 + \mathcal{O}(\partial^4)\right]$$

- **LPA (Local Potential Approximation):** keeps only $U_k(\phi)$ with $Z_k = 1$.
- **LPA':** adds a field-independent anomalous dimension via $Z_k$.
- **Higher orders:** $\partial^4$, field-dependent $Z_k(\phi)$, etc.

**2. Vertex Expansion**
Truncates the number of point-vertices $\Gamma^{(n)}$ retained (this is what your question emphasizes).

## Why η is Special

Here's the key point: **η is fundamentally tied to momentum dependence**. The anomalous dimension is defined through

$$\eta = -\partial_t \ln Z_k \big|_{k\to \text{fixed point}}$$

At the fixed point, $Z_k \sim k^{-\eta}$, encoding the deviation of the propagator from mean-field $1/p^2$ behavior toward $1/p^{2-\eta}$.

**Consequence:** In pure LPA (where $Z_k = 1$), you get **η = 0 identically**. You cannot capture the anomalous dimension without retaining field or momentum dependence in the two-point function. This is the most dramatic truncation effect.

## Concrete Numbers for the 3D Ising (Z₂ Scalar)

The exact/best-known value is **η ≈ 0.036**. Here's how truncations perform:

| Truncation | η | Notes |
|------------|-----|-------|
| LPA | 0 (by construction) | No momentum dependence |
| LPA' | ~0.11 | Constant Z_k; overshoots |
| DE O(∂²) | ~0.04 | Field-dependent Z(φ) |
| DE O(∂⁴) | ~0.033 | Close to best estimates |
| DE O(∂⁶) | 0.0356(5) | Balatas–Delamotte–Tissier state of the art |
| Conformal bootstrap | 0.0362978(20) | Reference "exact" |

## How Vertex Truncation Specifically Affects η

When you truncate the **number of vertices** (vertex expansion), the effects on η manifest as:

1. **Feedback loss:** η is driven by the momentum-dependence of $\Gamma^{(2)}(p)$, which is fed by $\Gamma^{(3)}$ and $\Gamma^{(4)}$ through the loop integral. Cutting the tower too early starves this feedback.

2. **Momentum resolution:** If you keep vertices but evaluate them only at zero momentum (a common simplification), you lose the very structure that generates η. Retaining full momentum dependence of a few vertices often outperforms keeping many vertices at zero momentum.

3. **Slow, non-monotonic convergence:** Unlike the correlation length exponent ν (which converges quickly and is already decent in LPA, ~0.65 vs. exact 0.63), η converges more slowly and can overshoot before settling.

## Practical Guidance

- **ν is "cheap," η is "expensive":** ν comes largely from the potential/scaling structure; η demands genuine momentum-dependent information.
- **Regulator dependence:** At finite truncation, results depend on the cutoff $R_k$. The **principle of minimal sensitivity (PMS)**—optimizing over regulator parameters—is standard for extracting reliable η.
- **Convergence estimates:** The Delamotte group has shown the DE behaves as an asymptotic series with an apparent expansion parameter ~1/9, allowing genuine error bars.

---

Would you like me to go deeper into any of these—for example, the explicit flow equations that generate η at O(∂²), the role of the regulator optimization, or how the vertex expansion compares quantitatively to the derivative expansion for this model?

# Abstract

We investigate the impact of vertex expansion truncation order on the estimation of the anomalous dimension η within the Nonperturbative Renormalization Group (NPRG) framework. Using the Ising universality class in three dimensions as a benchmark, we systematically compare low-order truncations of the effective average action against higher-order schemes that retain additional momentum-dependent vertex functions. Our results demonstrate that low-order approximations, while computationally efficient, introduce systematic biases in η due to incomplete resolution of the field-dependent propagator. Incorporating higher-order vertices substantially improves convergence, yielding η estimates in closer agreement with conformal bootstrap and Monte Carlo benchmarks. We quantify the residual truncation error and identify the minimal order required for reliable predictions. These findings clarify the interplay between truncation order and observable accuracy, offering practical guidance for balancing computational cost against precision in NPRG calculations of critical exponents.

# Abstract

We present a novel truncation scheme for the functional renormalization group (FRG) that incorporates all vertex functions simultaneously while systematically approximating their momentum dependence. Conventional approaches to nonperturbative renormalization group flows typically rely on either the derivative expansion, which sacrifices momentum resolution, or the Blaizot–Méndez-Galain–Wschebor (BMW) scheme, which requires closure approximations at a fixed vertex order. Our method overcomes these limitations by parametrizing the full hierarchy of one-particle-irreducible vertices through a self-consistent momentum-dependent ansatz, allowing the coupled flow equations to be closed without truncating the vertex expansion at finite order.

The central idea is to represent the momentum structure of higher-order vertices via a compact set of form factors whose flow is driven by the two-point function, thereby feeding back the full field dependence into the self-energy at every renormalization group scale. This construction preserves the analytic structure of the propagator while retaining sensitivity to nontrivial momentum configurations away from the symmetric point.

We benchmark the approach on the three-dimensional Ising universality class, focusing on the momentum-dependent self-energy and the associated anomalous dimension. Our results for the critical exponent η show quantitative agreement with high-precision Monte Carlo and conformal bootstrap determinations, while the computed self-energy exhibits the correct crossover between the infrared critical regime and the ultraviolet perturbative behavior. Comparison against BMW and higher-order derivative-expansion results demonstrates improved convergence and reduced regulator dependence.

The proposed framework offers a computationally tractable route to capturing full momentum dependence in strongly correlated systems and generalizes naturally to fermionic theories, dynamical critical phenomena, and out-of-equilibrium settings where the interplay of all vertices and finite-momentum effects is essential.
